options.a: Whether behavior occurred at any point in each interval
options.b: Every instance of the target behavior during observation
options.c: Whether behavior is occurring at the end of each interval
options.d: Behavior that lasts the entire interval being scored

distractorExplanations.a: Recording any occurrence within an interval is partial-interval recording, a discontinuous method, not continuous.
distractorExplanations.c: Checking at the end of each interval is momentary time sampling, a discontinuous method.
distractorExplanations.d: Scoring behavior that fills the whole interval is whole-interval recording, a discontinuous method.

options.a: Time from the instruction to the first response
options.b: Total time the behavior lasts
options.c: Time elapsed between two consecutive responses
options.d: Count of responses per observation period

distractorExplanations.a: Time from the instruction to response onset is latency, not frequency.
distractorExplanations.b: Total time engaged in the behavior is duration, not a count of responses.
distractorExplanations.c: Time between consecutive responses is interresponse time (IRT), not frequency.

options.a: How long a behavior lasts
options.b: How often a behavior occurs
options.c: How soon a behavior starts
options.d: Time between responses

distractorExplanations.b: How often a behavior occurs is frequency (a count), not duration.
distractorExplanations.c: How soon behavior starts after an SD is latency, not duration.
distractorExplanations.d: Time between consecutive responses is IRT, not how long each instance lasts.

options.a: Time from response onset to its offset
options.b: Time from SD/prompt to response onset
options.c: Time between two consecutive responses
options.d: Responses per minute of session

distractorExplanations.a: Onset to offset of a response is duration, not latency.
distractorExplanations.c: The time between consecutive responses is interresponse time (IRT), not latency.
distractorExplanations.d: Responses per minute is rate (frequency over time), not latency.

options.a: Time from the SD to the first response
options.b: Time from response onset to offset
options.c: Time between consecutive responses
options.d: Responses per unit of time

distractorExplanations.a: Time from the SD to the first response is latency, not interresponse time.
distractorExplanations.b: Onset to offset is the duration of one response, not the time between responses.
distractorExplanations.d: Responses per unit of time is rate, not interresponse time.

options.a: Behavior has clear onset and offset
options.b: Continuous recording is impractical
options.c: Exact counts of each response are needed
options.d: The behavior occurs only a few times daily

distractorExplanations.a: Discrete behaviors with clear onsets are good candidates for continuous recording, not a reason to switch methods.
distractorExplanations.c: Exact counts require continuous (event) recording; discontinuous methods only estimate occurrence.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-rate behaviors are easy to count continuously; discontinuous methods suit high-rate or long-lasting behaviors.

options.a: Overestimate occurrence for some behaviors
options.b: Underestimate occurrence for most behaviors
options.c: Match continuous duration data closely
options.d: Measure latency from the SD to response

distractorExplanations.b: Underestimation is the typical bias of whole-interval recording, not partial-interval recording.
distractorExplanations.c: Partial-interval scores any occurrence in an interval, so it inflates duration rather than matching it.
distractorExplanations.d: Partial-interval estimates occurrence; latency requires timing from the SD to response onset.

rbt-behavior-technician-readiness-check-.explanation: Overestimate occurrence relative to continuous for some behaviors. The overestimate is relative to continuous measurement, because any occurrence scores the whole interval.

options.a: Underestimate occurrence for some behaviors
options.b: Overestimate occurrence for some behaviors
options.c: Match frequency counts for brief behaviors
options.d: Record behavior only at the interval's end

distractorExplanations.b: Overestimation is the known bias of partial-interval recording, not whole-interval recording.
distractorExplanations.c: Whole-interval misses brief behaviors that do not fill an interval, so it does not match frequency counts.
distractorExplanations.d: Checking at the interval's end is momentary time sampling, not whole-interval recording.

options.a: Whether behavior occurred at any time during intervals
options.b: Whether behavior is occurring at the end of intervals
options.c: Whether behavior lasted throughout entire intervals
options.d: How many times behavior occurred in each interval

distractorExplanations.a: Any occurrence during the interval is partial-interval recording, not momentary time sampling.
distractorExplanations.c: Behavior lasting the whole interval is whole-interval recording, not momentary time sampling.
distractorExplanations.d: Counting occurrences within intervals is frequency (event) recording, not momentary time sampling.

options.a: Direct observation of each response as it occurs
options.b: Caregiver ratings of behavior after the session
options.c: Enduring environmental effects of behavior
options.d: Timing how long each response lasts

distractorExplanations.a: Watching each response live is continuous event recording; permanent product measures the outcome left behind.
distractorExplanations.b: Caregiver ratings are indirect assessment, not a tangible product of the behavior.
distractorExplanations.d: Timing each response is duration recording, not measuring a lasting product of behavior.

options.a: Based on the learner's diagnosis and inner feelings
options.b: Clear, objective, and complete enough for reliable measurement
options.c: Brief labels such as 'aggression' or 'tantrum'
options.d: Written by each RBT in their own words at the start of every session

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnoses and inner states are not observable; operational definitions describe observable, measurable behavior.
distractorExplanations.c: One-word labels are not operational; a definition must state observable examples and non-examples.
distractorExplanations.d: Definitions are set in the plan so all observers measure the same thing; personal rewording undermines IOA.

options.a: How well the intervention changes behavior
options.b: Whether the definition matches the diagnosis
options.c: Measurement agreement between observers
options.d: Consistency of the client's responding over time

distractorExplanations.a: Treatment effectiveness is judged by visual analysis of the data, not by IOA.
distractorExplanations.b: IOA checks agreement between observers' data, not alignment with a diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.d: Stability of the client's responding is variability in the data, not agreement between observers.

options.a: Components of interobserver agreement scores
options.b: Visual analysis features of graphed data
options.c: Steps of a task analysis for chaining
options.d: Dimensions of an operational definition

distractorExplanations.a: IOA is calculated with formulas such as total count or interval-by-interval; trend, level, and variability are graph features.
distractorExplanations.c: Task analysis steps are units of a skill, not properties of graphed data.
distractorExplanations.d: Operational definitions describe the behavior; trend, level, and variability describe data paths on a graph.

options.a: They show proportional change on a logarithmic multiply-divide scale
options.b: They support standard visual analysis of behavior change
options.c: They let the RBT skip operational definitions
options.d: They display cumulative totals that cannot go down

distractorExplanations.a: Logarithmic scaling describes standard celeration charts, not equal-interval line graphs.
distractorExplanations.c: No graph type replaces operational definitions; measurement depends on clear definitions.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-decreasing cumulative totals describe cumulative records, not equal-interval line graphs.

options.a: Supervisor direction within their scope
options.b: Their own clinical judgment once trained
options.c: Direction from the caregiver who hired them
options.d: Direction from a senior RBT on the team

distractorExplanations.b: Training does not grant independent clinical authority; RBTs assist under supervisor direction.
distractorExplanations.c: Caregivers can give input, but RBT assessment duties are directed by the BCBA/BCaBA supervisor.
distractorExplanations.d: A senior RBT is not a qualified supervisor; RBTs work under a BCBA, BCaBA, or other qualified supervisor.

options.a: Potential reinforcers
options.b: Behavior functions
options.c: Effective prompt levels
options.d: Mastery criteria

distractorExplanations.b: Behavior function is identified by a functional behavior assessment, not a preference assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Prompt levels are chosen through prompting procedures and data, not preference assessments.
distractorExplanations.d: Mastery criteria are set in the skill program by the supervisor, not found through preference assessment.

options.a: Choices made between two items at a time
options.b: Engagement when multiple items are available
options.c: Selections from an array with items removed
options.d: Caregiver rankings of the learner's favorites

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing between two items at a time is a paired-stimulus preference assessment, not free-operant.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing chosen items from an array is the MSWO procedure, not free-operant observation.
distractorExplanations.d: Caregiver rankings are an indirect preference assessment, not direct free-operant observation.

options.a: Antecedent, behavior, correction
options.b: Activity, baseline, compliance
options.c: Antecedent, behavior, consequence
options.d: Attention, behavior, communication

distractorExplanations.a: The C in ABC is consequence (what follows the behavior), not correction.
distractorExplanations.b: ABC stands for antecedent-behavior-consequence; activity, baseline, and compliance are unrelated terms.
distractorExplanations.d: Attention is one possible function, but the ABC acronym is antecedent, behavior, consequence.

options.a: Direct ABC observation during sessions
options.b: Interviews/checklists with caregivers
options.c: Functional analysis with test conditions
options.d: Scatterplot data recorded by the RBT

distractorExplanations.a: ABC observation in session is direct (descriptive) assessment, not indirect assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Manipulating test conditions is a functional analysis, an experimental method, not indirect assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Scatterplots are direct observational data, not indirect interview or checklist methods.

options.a: Variables maintaining problem behavior
options.b: The topography of problem behavior
options.c: A diagnosis that explains the behavior
options.d: Punishers that will stop the behavior

distractorExplanations.b: Topography describes what the behavior looks like; an FBA seeks why it continues (its maintaining variables).
distractorExplanations.c: Diagnosis is not the goal of an FBA; it identifies environmental variables maintaining the behavior.
distractorExplanations.d: An FBA identifies function to build function-based interventions, not punishers to suppress behavior.

options.a: Collect ABC data when assigned by a supervisor
options.b: Run preference assessments after training
options.c: Design comprehensive FBAs or behavior plans
options.d: Graph session data as directed by the plan

distractorExplanations.a: Collecting ABC data as assigned is a core RBT task; the prompt asks what RBTs do not do independently.
distractorExplanations.b: Conducting trained preference assessments is on the RBT Task List, so RBTs can do it.
distractorExplanations.d: Graphing data as directed is an RBT task; designing FBAs and behavior plans is the supervisor's job.

options.a: Caregiver satisfaction with services
options.b: The function of problem behavior
options.c: Current performance on targets
options.d: Learner item preferences

distractorExplanations.a: Satisfaction surveys measure social validity, not current performance on skill targets.
distractorExplanations.b: Function is identified by an FBA; skill probes check performance on acquisition targets.
distractorExplanations.d: Item preference is found through preference assessments, not skill probes.

options.a: After mastery to confirm the skill is maintained
options.b: Before intervention to describe current performance
options.c: During intervention to track response to treatment
options.d: After a reversal to show behavior returning

distractorExplanations.a: Post-mastery checks are maintenance probes, not baseline data.
distractorExplanations.c: Data collected during treatment is progress monitoring; baseline comes before intervention starts.
distractorExplanations.d: Return-to-baseline phases in a reversal design come later; initial baseline precedes any intervention.

options.a: The learner's diagnosis and IQ score
options.b: Topography and duration of the behavior
options.c: The reinforcement schedule in the plan
options.d: Setting, people, materials, time of day

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnosis and IQ are client characteristics, not ecological variables in the environment.
distractorExplanations.b: Topography and duration describe the behavior itself, not the surrounding ecological context.
distractorExplanations.c: Reinforcement schedules are programmed contingencies, not the ecological setting variables an RBT notes.

options.a: Shared with any staff member who asks
options.b: Discussed with family friends who help
options.c: Stored on a personal phone for easy access
options.d: Protected per ethics and employer policy

distractorExplanations.a: Client information goes to those who need it to deliver services, not to any staff member who asks.
distractorExplanations.b: Family friends are not authorized recipients unless the guardian consents in writing.
distractorExplanations.c: Storing client information on personal devices violates employer privacy policy unless approved and secured.

options.a: Flag for supervisor review; do not silently alter
options.b: Correct the numbers to match what you observed
options.c: Discard the session data and note it as missed
options.d: Ask the caregiver which record is accurate

distractorExplanations.b: Altering recorded data, even to match memory, falsifies records; report the discrepancy to the supervisor.
distractorExplanations.c: Deleting data hides the problem; inconsistencies go to the supervisor for review.
distractorExplanations.d: Caregivers do not resolve data integrity issues; the supervisor reviews inconsistent data.

options.a: RBT-written behavior plans
options.b: Supervised intervention planning
options.c: Diagnosis of the client's disorder
options.d: Caregiver-led treatment design

distractorExplanations.a: RBTs do not write behavior plans; the supervisor uses assessment results to plan intervention.
distractorExplanations.c: ABA assessment informs intervention, not a medical or psychological diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.d: Caregivers give input, but intervention design is the supervisor's responsibility.

options.a: Teaching within play using the learner's motivation and interests
options.b: Clear SD, response, consequence, and short intertrial intervals
options.c: Linking each step of a routine from the first step forward
options.d: Reinforcement delivered on a fixed-time schedule without a response

distractorExplanations.a: Embedding teaching in play around motivation is naturalistic teaching (NET), not DTT.
distractorExplanations.c: Teaching a routine step by step from the first is forward chaining, not discrete trial training.
distractorExplanations.d: Response-independent fixed-time delivery is noncontingent reinforcement, not DTT.

options.a: Increase reliance on the prompt
options.b: Thin the reinforcement schedule
options.c: Transfer stimulus control to the SD
options.d: Transfer stimulus control to the prompt

distractorExplanations.a: Prompt fading aims to reduce prompt dependence, not increase it.
distractorExplanations.b: Schedule thinning reduces reinforcement frequency; prompt fading reduces prompts.
distractorExplanations.d: Fading moves stimulus control away from the prompt and onto the natural SD.

options.a: An independent opportunity first
options.b: More intrusive prompts then fades
options.c: A gestural prompt, then adds help
options.d: A fixed time delay of 4 seconds

distractorExplanations.a: Starting with an independent opportunity is least-to-most prompting, the opposite order.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding help after a gesture is least-to-most; most-to-least starts with the most intrusive prompt.
distractorExplanations.d: Time delay is a separate prompting procedure; most-to-least starts with full assistance and fades.

options.a: Full physical guidance, then fades to less intrusive prompts
options.b: A 0-second delay prompt, then gradually lengthens the delay
options.c: Opportunity for independent response then increases assistance
options.d: Modeling the response, then fading to a gestural prompt

distractorExplanations.a: Starting with full physical guidance is most-to-least prompting, the opposite order.
distractorExplanations.b: Starting at 0 seconds and lengthening the delay is progressive time delay, not least-to-most.
distractorExplanations.d: Model-to-gesture fading moves from more to less help, which is most-to-least logic.

options.a: Future probability of the behavior it follows
options.b: Future probability of the behavior it precedes
options.c: The immediate intensity of the current behavior
options.d: Satiation for the stimulus delivered

distractorExplanations.b: Reinforcement acts on the behavior it follows; a stimulus that precedes behavior is an antecedent.
distractorExplanations.c: Reinforcement changes future likelihood, not the intensity of the response already occurring.
distractorExplanations.d: Satiation reduces a reinforcer's effectiveness; it is not what reinforcement increases.

options.a: After a skill is mastered
options.b: To promote resistance to extinction
options.c: During maintenance
options.d: When teaching new skills

distractorExplanations.a: Once a skill is mastered, schedules are thinned to intermittent reinforcement for maintenance.
distractorExplanations.b: Intermittent, not continuous, reinforcement builds resistance to extinction.
distractorExplanations.c: Maintenance uses thinned, intermittent schedules, not continuous reinforcement.

options.a: Maintain skills and resist extinction
options.b: Speed up acquisition of new skills
options.c: Make behavior extinguish faster
options.d: Replace the need for prompting

distractorExplanations.b: Continuous reinforcement speeds new learning; intermittent schedules support maintenance.
distractorExplanations.c: Intermittent schedules make behavior more resistant to extinction, not quicker to extinguish.
distractorExplanations.d: Reinforcement schedules do not replace prompting; prompts and fading address stimulus control.

options.a: Antecedent-behavior links
options.b: Discrete trials with SDs
options.c: Teachable component steps
options.d: Prompt hierarchy levels

distractorExplanations.a: Antecedent-behavior links come from ABC analysis, not from a task analysis.
distractorExplanations.b: Discrete trials are a teaching format; task analysis breaks a complex skill into steps.
distractorExplanations.d: A prompt hierarchy orders prompt intrusiveness; task analysis divides the skill itself into steps.

options.a: First step first, then adds subsequent steps
options.b: Last step first, then adds earlier steps
options.c: Every step in each trial until mastered
options.d: Steps in random order to build flexibility

distractorExplanations.b: Starting with the last step and working backward is backward chaining.
distractorExplanations.c: Teaching every step in each trial is total-task chaining, not forward chaining.
distractorExplanations.d: Chaining teaches steps in a set sequence; random order is not forward chaining.

options.a: Last step first with therapist completing earlier steps initially
options.b: First step first with therapist completing later steps initially
options.c: Every step in every trial with prompts as needed for each
options.d: The middle steps first because they are often the hardest

distractorExplanations.b: Teaching the first step and having the therapist finish the rest is forward chaining.
distractorExplanations.c: Prompting through every step in each trial is total-task chaining, not backward chaining.
distractorExplanations.d: Chaining starts at one end of the sequence; backward chaining begins with the last step.

options.a: Performance after teaching has stopped for weeks
options.b: Reduced prompts within the same teaching setting
options.c: Performance across people, settings, and stimuli
options.d: Faster responding to one specific SD in the clinic

distractorExplanations.a: Continued performance after teaching ends is maintenance, not generalization.
distractorExplanations.b: Prompt fading in one setting builds stimulus control, not generalization across people and settings.
distractorExplanations.d: Fluency with one SD in one setting is the opposite of generalization across stimuli.

options.a: Skills occur across new people and settings
options.b: Skills are acquired with as few errors as possible
options.c: Skills reach mastery criteria during teaching
options.d: Skills continue after teaching intensity reduces

distractorExplanations.a: Responding across new people and settings is generalization, not maintenance.
distractorExplanations.b: Minimizing errors during acquisition is errorless teaching, not maintenance.
distractorExplanations.c: Reaching mastery is acquisition; maintenance is what happens after teaching is reduced.

options.a: Let errors occur so correction can follow each one
options.b: Start with independent trials before any prompting
options.c: Increase speed of responding before accuracy
options.d: Minimize errors while establishing correct responding

distractorExplanations.a: Allowing errors and then correcting is an error-correction approach, not errorless teaching.
distractorExplanations.b: Starting with independent trials is least-to-most prompting, which allows errors.
distractorExplanations.c: Building speed before accuracy is a fluency goal, not errorless teaching's aim of preventing errors.

options.a: Rapid table-based trials with set SDs
options.b: Structured drills before free play time
options.c: Group lessons led by a classroom teacher
options.d: Ongoing activities and learner interests

distractorExplanations.a: Rapid structured table trials describe DTT, not naturalistic teaching.
distractorExplanations.b: Drills before play keep teaching separate from activities; NET embeds it within them.
distractorExplanations.c: Group instruction is a format, not naturalistic embedding in the learner's own activities and interests.

options.a: Follow the verbal instruction since it is more recent
options.b: Clarify with supervisor; follow the authorized plan
options.c: Ask the caregiver which version to follow
options.d: Blend both versions until the next supervision

distractorExplanations.a: Recency does not authorize a change; the RBT clarifies with the supervisor and follows the written plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Caregivers do not authorize program changes; the supervisor resolves conflicts in the plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixing versions risks inconsistent treatment; clarify with the supervisor and follow the authorized plan.

options.a: Their own independent RBT certification authority
options.b: A caregiver's direction in place of BACB supervision
options.c: Supervision only during their first year
options.d: Supervision requirements and BACB ethics standards

distractorExplanations.a: The RBT credential does not allow independent practice; RBTs must be supervised.
distractorExplanations.b: Caregivers cannot replace required supervision by a qualified BCBA, BCaBA, or other qualified supervisor.
distractorExplanations.c: RBT supervision is ongoing (at least 5% of service hours monthly), not limited to the first year.

rbt-behavior-technician-readiness-check-.explanation: Supervision requirements and BACB ethics standards applicable to their role. The standards are those applicable to the RBT role, including ongoing supervision of at least 5% of service hours each month.

options.a: Impair objectivity — avoid/manage per ethics
options.b: Strengthen rapport and should be encouraged
options.c: Be accepted if the family requests them
options.d: Be resolved by the RBT without telling anyone

distractorExplanations.b: Multiple relationships risk exploitation and lost objectivity; the code says avoid or manage them, not encourage them.
distractorExplanations.c: Family requests do not remove the conflict-of-interest risk of a multiple relationship.
distractorExplanations.d: Potential multiple relationships should be raised with the supervisor, not handled alone.

options.a: Required for billing but not ethics
options.b: An ethical and clinical requirement
options.c: Optional when the supervisor attends
options.d: Acceptable if completed days later

distractorExplanations.a: Accurate documentation is an ethics requirement too, not just a billing need.
distractorExplanations.c: Data and notes are still required when the supervisor is present.
distractorExplanations.d: Late notes risk inaccuracy; documentation should be timely as well as accurate.

options.a: Approved skill programs
options.b: Preference assessments you were trained on
options.c: Unauthorized restrictive procedures
options.d: Data collection procedures listed in the plan

distractorExplanations.a: Implementing supervisor-approved programs as written is exactly what RBTs should do.
distractorExplanations.b: Trained preference assessments are within the RBT scope, not something to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Collecting data per the plan is a core RBT duty, not a prohibited activity.

rbt-behavior-technician-readiness-check-.explanation: Unauthorized restrictive procedures outside the plan and law. Restrictive procedures outside the behavior plan and applicable law are off-limits.

options.a: Wait until you collect enough proof before reporting
options.b: Tell the caregiver first so they can explain
options.c: Report to your supervisor and let them decide
options.d: Follow mandated reporting and employer procedures

distractorExplanations.a: Mandated reporters report reasonable suspicion; they do not wait to gather proof.
distractorExplanations.b: Alerting the caregiver may endanger the child or compromise evidence; follow mandated reporting steps.
distractorExplanations.c: Telling a supervisor may be policy, but the mandated reporting duty is personal and cannot be delegated.

options.a: Create ethical issues — follow code/employer policy
options.b: Be accepted if declining would offend the family
options.c: Be fine if disclosed after the case ends
options.d: Be kept if valued under one hundred dollars

distractorExplanations.b: Fear of offending does not justify large gifts; follow the RBT Ethics Code and employer policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Gifts during services are the issue; later disclosure does not resolve the conflict.
distractorExplanations.d: Ethics guidance allows at most gifts of minimal value (the BACB code cites about $10), far below $100.

options.a: Using client first names in the waiting room
options.b: Sharing session wins in a private staff group chat
options.c: Posting de-identified session photos online
options.d: Not discussing client details in public spaces

distractorExplanations.a: Names discussed in shared spaces can identify clients; confidentiality means not discussing details publicly.
distractorExplanations.b: Even private chats with uninvolved staff can breach confidentiality; share on a need-to-know basis.
distractorExplanations.c: Photos can identify clients even without names; posting them breaches confidentiality.

options.a: Report data errors
options.b: Ask supervisors for clarification
options.c: Maintain their RBT certification
options.d: Misrepresent credentials

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting data errors promptly is required, not something RBTs avoid.
distractorExplanations.b: Seeking clarification from supervisors is expected professional behavior.
distractorExplanations.c: Maintaining certification (renewal, competency assessment) is required of RBTs, not prohibited.

options.a: Applying the same family goals to every client for fairness
options.b: Respecting family values while following ethical/clinical standards
options.c: Adopting any family practice even when it conflicts with ethics
options.d: Assuming a family's needs from their cultural background

distractorExplanations.a: Uniform goals ignore each family's values; cultural humility individualizes within ethical standards.
distractorExplanations.c: Respect for culture does not override ethical and clinical standards or client safety.
distractorExplanations.d: Stereotyping by background is the opposite of humility, which asks and learns from each family.

options.a: Are fine once services have ended
options.b: Are allowed if accounts are private
options.c: Need caution per ethics/employer rules
options.d: Should be accepted to build family rapport

distractorExplanations.a: Post-service contact can still create multiple-relationship risks; follow ethics and employer rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Private settings do not remove the dual-relationship and confidentiality risks of online connections.
distractorExplanations.d: Rapport is built in session; online friend requests from clients create dual-relationship risk.

options.a: Request training/supervision before implementing
options.b: Implement it while watching a training video
options.c: Implement it and ask for feedback afterward
options.d: Have a caregiver demonstrate it first

distractorExplanations.b: Videos do not replace competency-based training and supervision before implementing a procedure.
distractorExplanations.c: Training must come before implementation, not after, to protect the client.
distractorExplanations.d: Caregivers are not qualified trainers for clinical procedures; request training from the supervisor.

options.a: Arriving early but skipping notes on short sessions
options.b: Correcting caregivers in front of the client to model
options.c: Prepared materials but frequent last-minute cancellations
options.d: Punctuality, prepared materials, and respectful collaboration

distractorExplanations.a: Session notes are required for every session; professionalism includes complete documentation.
distractorExplanations.b: Public correction damages collaboration; feedback to caregivers should be respectful and private.
distractorExplanations.c: Reliable attendance is part of professionalism; frequent last-minute cancellations undermine it.
